guide.title: First time at the big mandals?
guide.subtitle: What the different lines mean, when to go, what to carry, and how to keep elders and kids safe.
guide.mukhBody: A view of the idol's face from a short distance. You keep walking past. It moves much faster and suits elders, children and anyone short on time.
guide.navasBody: For people who have made a vow (navas) and want to touch the idol's feet. At the most famous mandals this line can take many hours, sometimes most of a day or night.
guide.linesTip: Not sure which line you're in? Ask a volunteer before you join. Switching later means starting again.

sections.title: When to go
points: Early morning, roughly 4–7 am, is usually the quietest.
Evenings after 7 pm, weekends, the first day and the last days are the heaviest.
Check the wait range for the time you plan to go, and plan for the top end.

sections.title: What to carry
points: Water, and a small snack for long lines.
A charged phone and a power bank. Networks can slow down in thick crowds.
Some cash as well as UPI, for the same reason.
A raincoat or small umbrella. September showers are common.
Comfortable footwear you can walk in for hours.

sections.title: What to leave at home
points: Big bags. Large bags slow down security checks, and some mandals don't allow them.
Jewellery and valuables. Crowds attract pickpockets.
Keep your phone and wallet in a zipped front pocket.

sections.title: With elders and children
points: Plan for the top of the wait range, or choose mukh darshan.
Write your phone number on a card in your child's pocket, or on their arm.
Agree on a meeting point at a fixed landmark in case you get separated.
Keep children on the inside, away from barricades and road edges.
If someone feels unwell, step out of the line and tell a volunteer or police officer straight away.

sections.title: In a big crowd
points: Move with the flow. Don't stop suddenly, especially on stairs and bridges.
If the crowd starts pressing, keep your arms loosely in front of your chest to protect your breathing space.
Don't push to get ahead. Surges start small.
Follow the instructions of police and mandal volunteers.

sections.title: Getting there
points: Local trains and walking are usually the easiest. Parking near the big mandals is very limited and roads get closed.
Check the queue start pin, not just the mandal. Lines often begin far from the pandal.
Late at night, check which trains are still running before you join a long line.

guide.emergencyBody: Dial 112, India's national emergency number, or tell the nearest police officer or mandal volunteer. The big mandals run help and announcement desks for lost children and belongings.
